items.title: Gap Mangione interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012
items.q: But of course we were with Sal Nistico, Roy McCurdy, the band was not shy.

ctx.x: As a matter of fact I think Chuck and I both, although he did teach for a while, both in terms of semi-private or private lessons, and then of course he started the jazz program essentially at the Eastman School of Music. I think both of us had the idea that we would play until it didn’t work out so well, and then we would get a regular job. So far so good. There was never a, okay we’re going to go for this or we’re going to do that. The kinds of things that happen when you have a recording session and when you…
enough — we were too young to know enough to be scared. We shouldn’t have been there. But of course we were with Sal Nistico, Roy McCurdy, the band was not shy.

items.title: Roy McCurdy interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995
items.q: Chuck and Gap [Mangione]. Well after I came out of the service

ctx.x: How did you get hooked up with the Jazz Brothers?

Chuck and Gap [Mangione]. Well after I came out of the service, you know I went into the Air Force and then I came back and I was studying at the Eastman School of Music with Bill Street, a percussion teacher there. And I started working at a place called The Pythod which was a local jazz club up there. And they had a lot of people coming through. And Chuck and Gap were local musicians and I think Chuck had the band. He was leading one of the local bands and working in this club. So I think shortly after I got…
Didn’t he always invite the visiting musicians to Rochester over to his house?
